impacts.caseName: Teva Pharmaceuticals International GmbH v. Eli Lilly and Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in granting judgment as a matter of law that patent claims directed to using humanized anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies to treat headache were invalid for failure to satisfy the written-description and enablement requirements of 35 U.S.C. § 112.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's JMOL of invalidity for Teva's headache patents, which cover methods of treating headache using humanized anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies. The court found error in the invalidity determination despite the patents disclosing only one specific humanized antibody (G1, the active ingredient in Ajovy). This case implicates billions of dollars in the migraine therapeutic market involving Teva's Ajovy and Lilly's competing product.
impacts.positiveImplications: Strengthens patent holders' ability to obtain and enforce genus claims in the biologics space even when the specification discloses a limited number of species, potentially broadening patent protection for antibody-based therapeutics.
impacts.negativeImplications: Generic and biosimilar developers may face broader patent barriers to entry in the lucrative migraine/CGRP market and similar biologic therapeutic areas.

impacts.caseName: The Trustees of Columbia University v. Gen Digital Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to detecting anomalous program executions by comparing function calls in an emulator to a model are directed to an abstract idea under step one of the Alice framework, and whether damages based on foreign sales were properly awarded.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated a $185 million jury verdict for Columbia, holding that the asserted cybersecurity patent claims are abstract at Alice step one and remanding for step two analysis. The court also held the district court erred in allowing damages for foreign sales. The decision impacts patent eligibility for software-based cybersecurity inventions and extraterritorial damages.
impacts.positiveImplications: Provides technology companies a stronger basis to challenge cybersecurity and software-method patents under § 101, and limits patentees' ability to recover damages based on foreign product sales.
impacts.negativeImplications: Universities and other patent holders asserting software and cybersecurity patents face heightened § 101 vulnerability, and cannot readily capture foreign revenue in domestic patent damages calculations.

impacts.caseName: International Medical Devices, Inc. v. Cornell
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether there was legally sufficient evidence to support the jury's finding that asserted trade secrets were protectable under California law, and whether information that was generally known could constitute an inventive contribution for patent inventorship purposes.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the trade secret misappropriation verdict, finding insufficient evidence that the asserted trade secrets were protectable because the underlying information was generally known. The court also reversed the patent inventorship correction, vacated the reasonable royalty and exemplary damages, and dissolved the permanent injunction, while affirming the counterfeiting liability. This decision sets a high evidentiary bar for trade secret protectability under California law.
impacts.positiveImplications: Defendants in trade secret cases benefit from a rigorous standard requiring patent holders to prove that asserted trade secrets are not generally known in the field, reducing exposure to overbroad trade secret claims.
impacts.negativeImplications: Trade secret holders face heightened risk that their asserted secrets will be found unprotectable if the underlying information is generally available in the industry, even after obtaining a favorable jury verdict.

impacts.caseName: VLSI Technology LLC v. Intel Corporation
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether summary judgment of noninfringement was proper based on extraterritoriality principles where the accused multi-core processor selection method was performed partly outside the United States, and whether the district court properly struck damages theories for inadequate disclosure.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit addressed the extraterritorial reach of U.S. patent infringement law in the context of Intel's multi-core processors, reversing in part and affirming in part. The court's ruling on when method claims can reach conduct occurring partly outside the U.S. has significant implications for semiconductor and technology companies with global operations. The court also addressed the propriety of striking damages expert theories for disclosure deficiencies.
impacts.positiveImplications: Technology companies with globally distributed operations may benefit from limits on the extraterritorial application of U.S. method patent claims.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders asserting method claims against products designed or partly manufactured abroad face additional hurdles in proving domestic infringement.

impacts.caseName: Global Tubing LLC v. Tenaris Coiled Tubes LLC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether summary judgment was proper on inequitable conduct and Walker Process antitrust fraud claims where the patentee allegedly failed to disclose prior art (CYMAX documents) acquired through a corporate acquisition.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated summary judgment on both inequitable conduct and Walker Process fraud claims, finding genuine disputes of material fact on both issues. The court held that evidence regarding Tenaris's knowledge of and failure to disclose prior art CYMAX documents during patent prosecution precluded summary judgment. The Walker Process claim, which sought antitrust liability for attempted monopolization through fraud on the patent office, also survived.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers and competitors gain a stronger basis to assert inequitable conduct and Walker Process antitrust defenses when a patentee acquires prior art through corporate acquisitions and fails to disclose it during prosecution.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies that acquire businesses with legacy products must exercise heightened diligence in reviewing acquired documents for potential prior art relevance to pending or future patent applications, or face inequitable conduct and antitrust exposure.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to non-uniform constellations for digital communication systems are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court properly denied JMOL on infringement and damages.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated summary judgment of patent eligibility for some asserted claims while affirming eligibility for others, in a case involving digital broadcast communication standards used in televisions. The court affirmed the infringement and damages findings, including the denial of JMOL challenging the damages expert's testimony. This case is significant for standard-essential patent disputes in the consumer electronics industry.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders with claims tied to industry communication standards that include specific technical implementations beyond mathematical optimization may maintain eligibility, and damages methodologies tying royalties to standard adoption were upheld.
impacts.negativeImplications: Consumer electronics manufacturers face continued patent infringement exposure from standard-essential patents, and claims that are characterized as mathematical optimization may be found ineligible on remand.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the PTO Director's instructions to the Board governing the exercise of discretionary authority to decline institution of inter partes review proceedings constitute 'general statements of policy' exempt from notice-and-comment rulemaking under the APA.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed that the PTO Director's instructions on IPR institution discretion are general statements of policy exempt from APA notice-and-comment rulemaking requirements. The court emphasized that Congress gave the Director unreviewable discretion over institution and that the instructions do not bind the Director. This decision preserves the PTO's flexibility to manage IPR institution without formal rulemaking.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders benefit from the PTO retaining broad discretion to deny IPR institution, as the Director's policies limiting institution cannot be easily challenged procedurally.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology companies and other frequent IPR petitioners lose a procedural avenue to challenge PTO policies that restrict access to inter partes review, potentially leaving more patents unchallenged.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Board erred in its construction of claim terms in a patent covering systems and methods for streaming partly encrypted media content, specifically regarding the scope of 'encryption information.'
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the Board's claim construction in an IPR involving DivX's patent on streaming encrypted media content, vacated the Board's decision that Netflix failed to prove obviousness, and remanded. The decision impacts the streaming media industry by clarifying the scope of patent claims covering partial content encryption in adaptive bitrate streaming systems.
impacts.positiveImplications: Streaming services and content delivery networks benefit from a narrower construction of encryption-related patent claims, potentially freeing common streaming technologies from patent constraints.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders in the digital media streaming space may find their claims construed more narrowly, weakening enforcement positions against major streaming platforms.

impacts.caseName: Actelion Pharmaceuticals Ltd v. Mylan Pharmaceuticals Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the claim term 'a pH of 13 or higher' in pharmaceutical composition patents refers to a pH measured at a standard temperature in the field, and whether Actelion was barred from asserting infringement under the doctrine of equivalents.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed noninfringement of Actelion's epoprostenol formulation patents, holding that the claim term 'a pH of 13 or higher' refers to pH measured at the field-standard temperature of 25°C. The court also affirmed that Actelion was barred from asserting the doctrine of equivalents. This ruling clears the path for Mylan's generic version of Veletri® for pulmonary hypertension.
impacts.positiveImplications: Generic pharmaceutical manufacturers benefit from a clear ruling that pH claim limitations are measured at standard field temperatures, facilitating design-around strategies for generic drug formulations.
impacts.negativeImplications: Branded pharmaceutical companies face narrower claim scope when using measurement-based limitations in composition claims, potentially reducing their ability to block generic competition.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the on-sale bar of pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. § 102(b) requires that prior-art sales expressly disclose a device's functionality, and whether Rule 30(b)(6) corporate representative testimony is admissible at summary judgment even when the witness lacks personal knowledge.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed summary judgment of invalidity under the on-sale bar, holding that sales of a prior-art device need not expressly disclose the device's functionality to trigger § 102(b). The court also held that Rule 30(b)(6) deposition testimony is admissible at summary judgment even when the corporate representative lacks personal knowledge, as 30(b)(6) designees may testify based on information gathered from the organization.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from a broader application of the on-sale bar and easier use of corporate representative testimony to prove prior-art sales, strengthening invalidity defenses.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face greater invalidity risk from prior commercial sales even where the seller did not publicly disclose the full functionality of the product, and face challenges from corporate testimony by witnesses without firsthand knowledge.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court abused its discretion in excluding a patent plaintiff's damages expert report and granting summary judgment based on absence of a remedy.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the exclusion of Exafer's damages expert report and vacated summary judgment for Microsoft based on absence of a damages remedy. The court found that the district court improperly excluded the expert's opinions on the financial benefits of Microsoft's Azure SmartNIC technology. This ruling reinforces that patent plaintiffs must be given a fair opportunity to present damages theories and that premature exclusion of expert testimony can constitute reversible error.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent plaintiffs, particularly smaller entities suing large technology companies, benefit from greater protection against premature exclusion of damages evidence that could eliminate their case entirely.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers like Microsoft may face extended litigation and trial exposure where damages experts survive Daubert challenges that district courts would otherwise have resolved at summary judgment.

impacts.caseName: Apple Inc. v. International Trade Commission
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the ITC correctly found that Apple's importation and sale of Apple Watch models with blood oxygen measurement features violated Section 337 of the Tariff Act by infringing Masimo's patents on wearable pulse oximetry devices.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the ITC's finding that Apple violated Section 337 by importing Apple Watch models that infringed Masimo's patents on wearable blood oxygen measurement technology. The court upheld the ITC's domestic industry determination, validity rulings, and infringement findings, sustaining the limited exclusion order barring importation of the infringing watches. This high-profile decision impacts Apple's ability to sell its flagship wearable product with health-monitoring features.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders in the medical device and wearable technology space are strengthened in their ability to use ITC exclusion orders to block importation of infringing products, even against the world's largest companies.
impacts.negativeImplications: Major consumer electronics companies face significant business disruption from ITC exclusion orders affecting flagship products, and must carefully navigate patent clearance before incorporating health-monitoring features.

impacts.caseName: Ascendis Pharma A/S v. BioMarin Pharmaceutical Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a respondent in an ITC proceeding may obtain a mandatory stay of a refiled declaratory judgment action under 28 U.S.C. § 1659(a)(2) after having missed the deadline for seeking a stay in an earlier-filed action involving the same issues.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held that an ITC respondent cannot circumvent the mandatory stay deadline under § 1659(a)(2) by dismissing and refiling a declaratory judgment action. BioMarin, after missing the 30-day deadline in the original action, attempted to obtain a mandatory stay of Ascendis's refiled DJ action, but the court ruled this would undermine the statutory scheme designed to prevent gamesmanship in parallel ITC and district court proceedings.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders pursuing ITC investigations benefit from certainty that respondents cannot manipulate the mandatory stay provision through strategic refiling of district court actions.
impacts.negativeImplications: ITC respondents who miss the statutory deadline for seeking a mandatory stay cannot cure the deficiency by refiling declaratory judgment actions, limiting their strategic options in parallel proceedings.

impacts.caseName: National Veterans Legal Services Program v. United States
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly approved a $125 million class action settlement of claims that the federal judiciary charged excessive PACER fees, including the reasonableness of attorneys' fees and incentive awards to class representatives.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed approval of a $125 million settlement in a nationwide class action alleging the federal judiciary exceeded its statutory authority by using PACER fees to fund expenses unrelated to PACER. The court upheld the settlement terms, attorneys' fees, and incentive awards to nonprofit class representatives, rejecting a pro se objector's challenges. This decision provides precedent for class settlement approval standards in government overcharge cases and validates incentive awards to organizational class representatives.
impacts.positiveImplications: Organizations and frequent PACER users benefit from the reimbursement of excessive fees, and the ruling supports the viability of class actions challenging government fee overcharges under the Little Tucker Act.

impacts.caseName: Willis Electric Co., Ltd. v. Polygroup Ltd. (Macao Commercial Offshore)
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly denied JMOL of obviousness and a new trial on damages for a patent covering pre-lit artificial trees with integrated mechanical and electrical connections.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the denial of JMOL of obviousness and a new trial on damages for Willis Electric's patent on pre-lit artificial Christmas trees with automatic electrical connections upon mechanical assembly. The court upheld the jury's findings against Polygroup's obviousness challenge, reinforcing that the combination of integrated mechanical-electrical connections at any rotational orientation was not obvious over the prior art. This decision has implications for the competitive holiday decorations market.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders in consumer product industries benefit from the court's rigorous application of the obviousness standard, protecting innovative product designs from challenges based on individual prior art elements.
impacts.negativeImplications: Consumer product manufacturers and importers face sustained patent infringement liability where their products replicate patented integration features, even in seemingly simple product categories.
